newsitem.title: GERMANY: Solid plan to fill Bonn tax gap crucial to markets.
newsitem.headline: Solid plan to fill Bonn tax gap crucial to markets.

text.p: German financial markets are gearing up for the potential bombshell of May tax revenue estimates next week, and analysts said on Friday that Bonn must act promptly to avoid serious damage to Bunds and the mark.

With predictions the shortfall in 1997 revenues could be as much as 20 billion marks, Finance Minister Theo Waigel will be under immediate pressure to present plans to generate cash and make up around 0.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The debate about the shortfall has moved to centre stage in German politics as the Kohl government scrambles to trim its budget deficit to qualify for Europe's currency union scheduled to begin in 1999.

If Waigel fails to provide solutions immediately, investors could turn against the mark and Bunds and undermine confidence in Germany's ability to meet the 3.0 percent deficit/GDP target for monetary union.

"You can't say to the people 'our revised forecasts show that the deficit will not meet 3.0 percent target' and then just leave it at that," said Gerlof de Vrij, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.

If detailed and credible saving plans are not put forward, economists say the mark, which has only just begun to struggle back from months of weakness against the dollar, could be in for another beating.
"I would be very surprised if they were not to make an immediate comment assuring us that everthing is under control," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
"But they will probably leave the details for later disclosure."

Waigel has said further measures will have to be taken to hit the government's forecast for 2.9 percent deficit/GDP ratio ratio, warning that tax revenues will show a shortfall of more than 10 billion marks from estimates made last November.
But man economists believe the government is more likely to find itself 17 to 20 billion marks out of pocket.
Waigel said this week that he intended to pursue spending cuts rather than tax increases to generate extra cash, but economists said the markets will only be pacified by hard, detailed proposals.

"Waigel has admitted that further measures will be needed... however, his rambling over a budget moratorium or further recepits from privatisation suggest that he has no clue where to find the money," one analyst said in a research note.
Waigel has said a complete freeze on new spending cannot be ruled out -- a drastic sounding move but one that economists say is unlikely to yield more than two to three billion marks in savings.
A hike in petrol prices is another possible move, with economists saying a 15 to 20 pfennig rise per litre could be on the cards.
Economists also said that as inflation remains below the Bundesbank's medium-term two percent target, a petrol increase would be relatively harmless for inflation, making it a popular option.

"They have talked about cutting social security further, but I simply don't think they will be able to do that -- it will be blocked partly by resistance within their own parties, and also by the upper house of parliament," said Schmieding.

With Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition hampered by public hosility to further cuts in social welfare to make the EMU grade, and well aware that any radical tax or spending moves would be stopped in their tracks by the opposition-dominated upper house, the answer among economists as to what more the government can do is "not much".
"The government just doesn't have much leeway," said ABN AMRO's de Vrij.
